name: The Reliability of the Biblical Text

objectives.text: Identify the Bible as one book made up of many smaller books that God gave through people who wrote down his words
Retell the account of King Jehoiakim burning Jeremiah's scroll and God having his words written down again
Describe how scribes copied God's Word by hand onto scrolls with great care
Distinguish a true account of real events from a made-up story using Luke's and Peter's descriptions of how they wrote
Recite Bible verses that promise God's Word will endure forever
Explain what an ancient manuscript is and that thousands of handwritten copies of the Bible still exist today
Identify the materials and forms ancient writers used, including papyrus, parchment, scrolls, and codices
Describe archaeological discoveries that confirm people and places named in the Bible, such as the Pool of Siloam, the Pilate Stone, and the Tel Dan inscription
Explain that the Bible was first written in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek and that the church translates it into the common language of every people
Compare the number of surviving manuscripts and the time gap to the earliest copies for the New Testament with other ancient works such as those of Homer, Caesar, and Tacitus
Describe the methods Jewish scribes and the Masoretes used, such as counting letters and words, to preserve the Hebrew text
Analyze the telephone game objection by explaining how many independent lines of copies allow scholars to compare manuscripts and recover the original wording
Explain the significance of the Dead Sea Scrolls by comparing the Great Isaiah Scroll with the Masoretic Text copied about a thousand years later
Explain why the New Testament writings being composed within the lifetime of eyewitnesses supports their historical accuracy
Describe the history of the English Bible from Wycliffe and Tyndale through the King James Version to modern translations
Classify textual variants by type, such as spelling, word order, and meaningful and viable readings, and explain how few affect meaning
Distinguish differences between English translations from variants that arose in the copying of manuscripts
Apply basic principles of textual criticism to bracketed passages noted in English Bibles such as the longer ending of Mark and the account of the adulterous woman
Construct a case for the reliability of the biblical text using bibliographical, internal, and external tests
Explain the Reformed teaching that Scripture's authority rests on God its author and how external evidences relate to the Spirit's witness
Distinguish the inspiration of the original writings from God's providential preservation of the text through copies as the Westminster Confession teaches
Evaluate Bart Ehrman's argument that textual variants undermine confidence in the New Testament
Evaluate conspiracy claims that the church altered the Bible at Nicaea using manuscripts that predate the council, such as P52, P66, and P75
Compare the Textus Receptus and modern critical texts by explaining the Byzantine and Alexandrian manuscript families behind them

changes: Kept and reworded real competencies on scribes, manuscript counts, archaeology, the telephone objection, the Dead Sea Scrolls, eyewitness dating, translation versus transmission, the three tests, Ehrman, conspiracy claims, and English Bible history, now split from manuscript families. Dropped 'apply confidence in the Bible' because it targets inner belief, and recast 'stories really happened' as distinguishing history from fiction using Luke 1:1-4 and 2 Peter 1:16. Added the Bible as many inspired books, Jeremiah's rewritten scroll, ancient writing materials, original languages and vernacular translation, Masoretic methods, variant classification, textual criticism of bracketed passages, the Reformed view of evidence and authority, and inspiration of the originals versus providential preservation. Anchored these to WCF 1.2, 1.4, 1.5, 1.8 and WSC Q2. Left resurrection, miracle, and prophecy evidence to the sibling sub-topics.
